_meta.name: English
admin.access.changed: It is presenting a different key than the one this stack trusts.
admin.access.changed_help: Either that machine was rebuilt, or something is answering in its place. This page will not guess which. Confirm on the machine itself before trusting the new one.
admin.access.confirm: Type the presented fingerprint to trust it
admin.access.confirm_help: The SHA256:… part, copied from the line above. Typed rather than clicked, because trusting a changed key is the one thing here that can hand a session to somebody else.
admin.access.confirm_mismatch: That did not match. Type {fingerprint} exactly.
admin.access.heading: Reaching the other machines
admin.access.intro: Only interesting when part of this stack runs somewhere else. A role pointing at this machine needs none of it — the deployer skips ssh entirely for those.
admin.access.key_absent: No key yet. Without one this page cannot reach any other machine.
admin.access.key_exists: A key already exists. Replacing it would lock this page out of every machine that trusts the old one, so this refuses.
admin.access.key_heading: The key this page deploys with
admin.access.key_import: Use a key you already have
admin.access.key_import_help: Paste the private half. It is checked by deriving the public one — which is also how a paste that lost its line breaks is caught. A key with a passphrase is refused: every connection here runs unattended and nothing could unlock it.
admin.access.key_import_replaces: There is already a key. Importing replaces it, which locks this page out of every machine that trusts the old one. The old key is kept on disk beside the new one.
admin.access.key_imported: The key was imported. Check the fingerprint above is the one you expect.
admin.access.key_install_help: Append that line to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on each machine below, for the user shown beside it.
admin.access.key_invalid: That is not a private key this can use — either it is malformed, or it has a passphrase.
admin.access.key_made: A key was generated. Put the public line on each machine below.
admin.access.key_present: A key exists. The private half is never read here and never shown.
admin.access.no_remotes: Every role points at this machine, so nothing here needs ssh.
admin.access.trusted: Its key is the one this stack trusts.
admin.access.two_identities: This page deploys with the key in {dir}. A deploy run from a terminal uses that account's own ~/.ssh instead, so the two can disagree — the container has no business reading somebody's personal keys.
admin.access.unknown: This stack holds no key for it yet.
admin.access.unknown_help: Check the fingerprint against the machine itself — `ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub` there — before trusting it.
admin.access.unreachable: {address} did not answer, so there is no key to compare.
admin.access.user_bad: That is not an account name, or the role is not one this stack knows.
admin.access.user_help: The account on that machine. It needs a shell and access to the docker socket: deploying means copying a tree there and running docker compose.
admin.apk.beta_help: The same build under a different name, for trying something before everyone gets it. It is not a separate app — installing it replaces the release on the phone.
admin.apk.failed: The build failed. The log above says where.
admin.apk.heading: Alfred app
admin.apk.intro: Builds the Android app from the source in this repository and puts it on the family share, where anyone can install it. Takes a few minutes; the first build after an update takes longer.
admin.apk.no_image: The builder image does not exist yet, so a build will fail. Create it once with: docker build -t alfred-app-builder:latest deploy/alfred-app/ — it takes a few minutes and about a gigabyte.
admin.apk.release_help: The normal one. Lands in familia/ on the share, replacing the previous copy, and updates what the app's own updater offers.
admin.apk.success: Built and copied to the family folder.
admin.auth.expired: Your session expired. Reload the page and sign in again.
admin.auth.locked: Too many attempts. Try again in {n} minutes.
admin.auth.locked_sub: Sign in to change how the house runs.
admin.auth.password_hint: At least {n} characters. It is stored as a hash; there is no way to recover it, only to replace it.
admin.auth.setup_sub: Nothing else on this page answers until you do. This page edits the household's settings and credentials, so treat the password as you would the key to the house.
admin.backups.archives_intro: The runs kept in this household's backup directory, newest first.
admin.backups.confirm_mismatch: That did not match. Type {service} exactly to confirm.
admin.backups.derived_note: Read from deploy/manifest.yml, not kept by hand here — so this page and ./home-stack backup cannot disagree about what matters. Paths are the real ones for this install.
admin.backups.encryption_intro: Every archive contains the credentials file and every password hash. Encrypt it if it leaves this machine — and it should leave this machine.
admin.backups.error_note: The list could not be computed. Everything else on this page is still whatever was readable.
admin.backups.group_bulk_intro: Recordings and scanned documents. Hundreds of gigabytes and mostly unchanged between runs, so no archive takes them -- point whatever uploads your backups at these directories directly.
admin.backups.group_essential_intro: Lose these and something is gone for good: the user store, the databases, the assistants' memory.
admin.backups.group_skipped_intro: Regenerable, and listed anyway: whether something is in the archive should be visible rather than inferred.
admin.backups.heading: What to back up
admin.backups.intro: Every directory and file that holds something this house cannot regenerate, with the machine it lives on and what it takes up today.
admin.backups.key_absent: No key yet. Encryption cannot be turned on without one.
admin.backups.key_exists: A key is already set. Replacing it would make every archive already written unreadable, so this refuses. Change it on the Credentials screen if that is really what you want.
admin.backups.key_made: A key was generated. Copy it off this machine now — Credentials can show it.
admin.backups.key_present: A key is set. It is not shown here and cannot be read back; the Credentials screen can reveal it.
admin.backups.key_warning: Keep a copy of the key somewhere this house burning down does not affect. An encrypted archive without its key is noise.
admin.backups.need_key: Generate a key first. Turning this on without one makes every run fail at the last step, after it has copied everything.
admin.backups.own_root: ./home-stack backup writes its own archives to {path}, which is not in the list above — backing up a backup is not the point.
admin.backups.own_tool_intro: The same list, one path per line, ready to paste into whatever you already use.
admin.backups.restore_confirm: Type the service name to confirm
admin.backups.restore_confirm_help: Typed rather than ticked, because this cannot be undone.
admin.backups.restore_intro: This overwrites live state with the copy in the archive. One service at a time: putting the whole archive back would also revert the user store and the credentials file, signing the house out and undoing every setting changed since. That one belongs at a terminal.
admin.backups.restore_note: Stop the service first if you can: a container holding a database open can write over part of what lands. Nothing reads what was restored until that service is deployed again.
admin.backups.restore_service_help: Only the services this archive actually holds. An older one may predate a service entirely.
admin.backups.run_help: Written to {path}. It verifies itself before it finishes.
admin.backups.test_intro: Unpack an archive into a scratch directory and check what came out. Nothing live is touched. Tick services to check only those; leave them all unticked to check the whole archive.
admin.backups.test_note: A narrowed run does not mark the archive verified: “home-paperless restores” is not the claim that marker makes. Use Verify in the table above for that.
admin.backups.test_services_help: Only what this archive actually holds is offered — an older one may predate a service entirely.
admin.backups.uncaptured_intro: Declared state that no backup here can copy. Naming a hole is not filling it — but an archive that quietly omits it reads exactly like one that does not.
admin.cloud.acme_provider_help: The acme.sh DNS plugin for your registrar (dns_cf, dns_hostinger, …). Only used in public-certificate mode.
admin.cloud.heading: Outside connections
admin.cloud.intro: All optional. The stack is fully usable without any of them.
admin.cloud.tunnel_port_help: Where the reverse tunnel from this machine lands on the VPS loopback. The proxy has no other route home.
admin.cloud.vps_help: Lets you reach the assistant from outside the house. Off by default.
admin.cloud.vps_managed_help: Deploying it means copying a tree there and running docker compose, which needs an account with a shell and access to the docker socket. A VPS set up by hand often has only an account that holds a reverse tunnel open and refuses to run anything. Unticked, the proxy stays configured and deploys stop trying — and say so once per run, rather than failing every time for a reason you have already accepted.
admin.cloud.vps_test_auth: The VPS answered but refused the key. Add this stack's public key to its authorized_keys.
admin.cloud.vps_test_help: Uses this stack's deploy key. To generate, import or authorise it:
admin.cloud.vps_test_hostkey: The VPS presents a different host key than the one trusted. Confirm it on Access before deploying.
admin.cloud.vps_test_nokey: There is no deploy key yet. Generate or import one on Access.
admin.cloud.vps_test_ok: Connected. This machine can reach the VPS.
admin.cloud.vps_test_unreachable: No answer from that address. Check the host, the network and that ssh is listening.
admin.cloud.vps_test_unset: No address set for the VPS yet.
admin.custom.description_placeholder: one line, shown under the name
admin.custom.heading: Links
admin.custom.icon_help: An emoji. The dashboard draws it as text, so an icon-set name would appear as a word.
admin.custom.intro: Anything else you run that deserves a tile on the portal: a NAS, a media server, the printer's page. Nothing here is built, deployed or checked — it is a bookmark. Applied on the portal's next deploy.
admin.custom.lan_only: Only reachable on the house network
admin.custom.lan_only_forced: A link written as http://address:port is house-only whichever way this box is set: the cloud proxy forwards the portal and nothing else, so those addresses never answer from outside. The box matters for links written as a path the portal serves.
admin.custom.lan_only_help: Tick this for anything on a private address — 192.168.x, 10.x, or a name only the house resolves. The tile is then left out for anyone opening the portal from outside, rather than offering a link that cannot open.
admin.custom.lan_only_note_app: In the Alfred app, “from the house network” means the app reached this machine rather than the cloud proxy — the app always uses the public address, so that only happens if the house resolver answers that name with this machine's address. Without that the app is treated as away and these tiles never appear in it, however close the phone is.
admin.custom.lan_only_note_what: This decides where the link is shown, not who can reach the service. What keeps a service private is its address: nothing on 192.168.x is reachable from outside, because the cloud proxy forwards only the portal. Leaving this unticked on a private address does not expose anything — it just draws a link that times out.
admin.custom.lan_only_note_where: Ticked, the tile is hidden from the portal dashboard and from Alfred's Apps menu whenever the request did not come from the house network, and carries a “casa” badge when it is shown. Untick it only for something genuinely reachable from anywhere.
admin.custom.name: Name
admin.deploy.blocked_alt: Or give a role the machine's real address, and this page will reach it over ssh with the keys it already mounts. Everything else here — saving settings, credentials, members — works as it is.
admin.deploy.blocked_container: Deploying from this page is refused: {roles} point at 127.0.0.1, which inside this container is the container. Deploy from a shell on the host.
admin.deploy.blocked_heading: Deploying has to come from the host
admin.deploy.blocked_intro: This page runs in a container, and {roles} point at 127.0.0.1 — which in here is the container, not the machine your services run on.
admin.deploy.blocked_why: Containers would start, because the Docker socket is mounted. That is what makes it worth refusing: the work would land on one machine and the checking on another. Run this in a terminal instead:
admin.deploy.heading: Deploy
admin.deploy.intro: Nothing here is automatic. A change is saved and waiting until you deploy it.
admin.deploy.no_self: This page cannot deploy itself. Run ./home-stack deploy admin from a terminal on the host.
admin.deploy.pending_services: {n} service(s) are running against an older configuration:
admin.deploy.self_help: «{name}» is this page. It cannot deploy itself — bringing it down is the first thing a deploy does, and the deploy is running inside it. «All» skips it. Redeploy it from a shell: ./home-stack deploy {name}
admin.members.add_help: A new id is generated and never reused. Their credentials are minted here.
admin.members.finance_bad-secret: PROXY_SHARED_SECRET contains a colon, which is the separator this token is built with. Rotate it on the Secrets page.
admin.members.finance_help: The token the finance dashboard asks for. Derived from the house secret and this person's portal login, so it is the same value every time and nothing is stored — press it again whenever you need it.
admin.members.finance_no-login: This person has no portal login yet, and the token is derived from one. Give them a login above first.
admin.members.finance_no-secret: PROXY_SHARED_SECRET is not set, so there is nothing to derive from. Generate it on the Secrets page.
admin.members.finance_shown: Shown once. Copy it now; leaving this page is enough to lose it.
admin.members.folder_clash: That name shares a file-share folder with {name}. Give one of them a name that differs by more than accents or spacing.
admin.members.heading: Household
admin.members.id_help: Generated. Never a national identity number.
admin.members.intro: Who lives here. Each person gets their own assistant, their own history and their own settings.
admin.members.login_password_required: A new account needs a password.
admin.members.login_password_short: The password has to be at least {n} characters.
admin.members.login_renamed: Saved, and their conversations were carried across.
admin.members.login_taken: Another member already signs in with that name.
admin.members.only_here: This is the only place household members are managed. Ids are never reused, so a removed person's credentials and history can never be inherited by someone new.
admin.members.paperless_deferred: {id} was registered, but their Paperless token could not be issued yet ({detail}). Use the Paperless button on this page once the archive is running.
admin.members.paperless_error: Could not create the token — is home-paperless deployed and running? ({detail})
admin.members.paperless_help: Create this person's document-archive account and API token in one step. Safe to press again — it returns the same token.
admin.members.paperless_ok: Paperless token for {id} created and stored. It reaches the assistant on the next deploy.
admin.members.phone_code_error: Could not issue a code — is the proxy deployed and running? ({detail})
admin.members.phone_code_help: A one-time code to enroll this person's phone in the chat app.
admin.members.phone_code_note: Valid for 10 minutes, single use. Enter it in the app's code field on the phone.
admin.members.remove_confirm: Remove {name}? Their assistant history stays on disk.
admin.models.about_role: What this job is, and what else fits
admin.models.advice.caches: publishes a cached-input price, and {share}% of this role’s input is cached
admin.models.advice.kind_unknown: the catalogue does not say whether it is the kind this role wants
admin.models.advice.local: on your own hardware — nothing per token, nothing leaves the house
admin.models.advice.no_cache: no cached-input price, so the {share}% of this role’s input that is cached bills at the full rate
admin.models.advice.no_reasoning: documented not to reason, and this role wants one that does
admin.models.advice.no_thinking: does not reason — right for this role, where thinking spends the budget and answers nothing
admin.models.advice.reasons: reports that it reasons, which this role wants
admin.models.advice.thinks: reasons, and this role must not: it spends the whole budget thinking and returns an empty answer
admin.models.advice.tight: {context}k context, barely over what this role requires
admin.models.advice.unknown_limits: reports no context or output limit, so nothing here can promise it fits
admin.models.advice.unpriced: publishes no price, so this cannot be estimated
admin.models.advice.writes_long: writes up to {tokens}k tokens, which this role needs
admin.models.advice.writes_short: writes at most {tokens}k tokens, short for this role
admin.models.assumed_short: No usage recorded yet, so prices assume a million input tokens a month.
admin.models.bench_failed: The run failed — see the log.
admin.models.bench_intro: Runs a model through a real assistant — its prompt, skills and Home Assistant tools — on this house's own work: everyday chat, tool calls, notification triage, events and the heartbeat. Anything that would change the house (lights, lists, messages, reminders) is recorded, not done. It shares the GPU with the family's model while it runs, and unloads the tested model when it finishes.
admin.models.bench_kind_background_help: Notifications, events and heartbeats: short, unattended jobs
admin.models.bench_kind_longtask_help: Background tasks that research and deliver a file
admin.models.bench_merged_help: Built from {n} runs: each role shows the most recent time it was measured.
admin.models.bench_model_help: Written like the pickers above (ollama:…, together:…, a bare name for OpenCode Zen), or a Hugging Face link. A Hugging Face repo must be GGUF; it is pulled into Ollama first, at Q4_K_M unless you add :QUANT.
admin.models.bench_params_help: Parameter count, from Ollama where the name does not say.
admin.models.bench_remove_confirm: Delete {model} from Ollama? It frees the disk; pulling it again takes as long as the first time.
admin.models.bench_remove_refused: Not removed: {model} is in use, or is not a local model.
admin.models.bench_shared_help: Ran on the family's Ollama: every case and every family turn swapped one model for the other, so these timings are pessimistic.
admin.models.bench_stale_cases_help: Scored by a different version of the test cases than the one on disk now, so it is not comparable with runs below it. Re-run to compare.
admin.models.bench_stale_setup_help: Made with skills, prompts or assistant code that have changed since, in the assistant it ran inside -- or before runs recorded that -- so it is not comparable with runs made now. Re-run to compare.
admin.models.bench_stub_note: * recorded by the benchmark and not executed — it would have changed something in the house.
admin.models.bench_tok_s_calls: Output tokens over the time spent in model calls (includes prompt processing).
admin.models.bench_tok_s_probe: Measured by Ollama: generation speed, and prompt processing on a 2k-token prompt.
admin.models.chain_edit_note: Tried in this order when a turn's model fails. Leave a place empty to drop it.
admin.models.chain_note: Tried in order. Edit this one in the config file — a picker cannot express a chain.
admin.models.chain_probe_why: each rescue model in order: every one a failing turn may land on has to answer
admin.models.code_help: Only this space may use a flat-plan model: it is one person at a keyboard, which is what that plan is for. Left unset, opencode picks — on this account that means a free model, whose terms allow training on what it reads.
admin.models.code_intro: Which model answers in the Code space, where the Programmer actually edits and runs things.
admin.models.code_no_roster: No roster yet — press Refresh above.
admin.models.code_off: The Code space is switched off, so nothing reads this yet.
admin.models.code_unknown: Not saved: {model} is not on this account's roster.
admin.models.compat_help: Anything that speaks the OpenAI API at an address you give it — vLLM, llama.cpp, LM Studio, or a hosted provider. With or without a trailing /v1.
admin.models.compat_key_note: OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_KEY, under credentials. Optional — a server on your own LAN usually wants none.
admin.models.freetoken_help: A FreeToken server on your own hardware. Point at it; this stack never deploys it.
admin.models.freetoken_key_note: Key (optional): FREETOKEN_API_KEY on the Secrets page. A server on your own desk usually needs none.
admin.models.go_refused: Not saved for {roles}: a flat-plan model is only for the Code space.
admin.models.group_conversation: Alfred, and what it starts itself
admin.models.group_conversation_why: The turn somebody is waiting for, and the background work handed off from it. A sub-agent sits under the model it is a sub-agent of, because leaving it blank is how it follows that model.
admin.models.group_profession_why: Each names one model and uses it. A turn inside one never falls back to the general models above.
admin.models.group_special_why: Not jobs: one is about what the turn contains, the other about what happens when a model stops answering.
admin.models.group_unattended: The house acting on its own
admin.models.group_unattended_why: Nobody is waiting. What decides where these can run is not speed but how much context each one carries — only the one that stays short can live on your own hardware.
admin.models.harness_allow_go: Allow OpenCode Go models in pi
admin.models.harness_allow_go_help: Lets the two sub-agent roles above pick a Go model, which only pi runs. Go is OpenCode's flat plan for interactive use, and background tasks are not that: OpenCode says traffic like this can get the account blocked. Off, a Go model is refused here.
admin.models.harness_enabled: Use the pi harness for background tasks
admin.models.harness_intro: A member's own background tasks -- research, a report, a spreadsheet -- run in pi, a small agent harness, with the sub-agent model above (the powerful sub-agent's for a complex task). A small prompt and four tools instead of Alfred's whole setup: local models do far better there. A question from someone else or from WhatsApp stays on Alfred's own loop.
admin.models.heading: Which model answers as which persona
admin.models.images_intro: Two slots, both in the cloud: nothing here runs on your own hardware. Left empty, the assistant says it cannot draw rather than quietly using whatever it shipped with.
admin.models.images_none_available: No image model is available. Add a key for a provider that has one — Together, OpenAI or OpenRouter — on the Secrets page, then refresh the list above.
admin.models.intro: Each persona does different work, so the model that suits one is wasteful or wrong for another. Saved here and applied to the assistant on the next deploy.
admin.models.invalid_url: That address is not a URL the stack can call. It needs http:// or https:// and a host — for example http://192.168.1.20:8000/v1. Nothing was saved.
admin.models.keyed_sources_note: OpenRouter, Together AI and OpenAI appear as soon as their key is set under credentials, and disappear when it is cleared. There is nothing else to configure: an account either reaches them or it does not.
admin.models.local_preferred: local is the right answer here
admin.models.local_refused: Not saved for {roles}: no local model can do it yet. Add a model setup on the Ollama card first.
admin.models.local_runs: Runs {setup} -- change it on the Ollama card below.
admin.models.not_priced_yet: Not priced yet — press Check now above, or wait for the scheduled check.
admin.models.ollama_advanced: Advanced: the general and benchmark servers
admin.models.ollama_advanced_help: The installer's own server loads whatever it is asked for: pulls, Paperless's embeddings, and any task not yet moved to a setup. The benchmark runs on its own.
admin.models.ollama_apply_sent: Sent to the host. Servers restart one by one.
admin.models.ollama_bench: The benchmark's server: whatever model is being benchmarked, one at a time.
admin.models.ollama_chain_not_followed: Left in the fallback chain as it was, because its setup now runs a model that cannot stand in: {roles}. The chain is edited in the config file.
admin.models.ollama_cloud_help: ollama.com. Needs OLLAMA_API_KEY, and what you send it leaves your network.
admin.models.ollama_fallback_is_everyday: The fallback chain now names the everyday model itself ({model}): a failing everyday turn would fall back to the model that just failed.
admin.models.ollama_gpu_help: The cards and what else runs on them are from the host's last look ({at}); each server's share is estimated from its model's size and window, or measured.
admin.models.ollama_gpu_over: Does not fit: lower a window or the slots, keep fewer models loaded, or move a server to another card.
admin.models.ollama_intro: A setup is one model at its own window, cache and slots, on Ollama or llama.cpp. Only setups a role uses run; pick them in the role pickers above. Preview shows how they land on the cards before you save.
admin.models.ollama_local_help: The role it runs on and its port. Nothing leaves the house and there is no per-token bill.
admin.models.ollama_measure_idle: Nothing runs on this server to measure.
admin.models.ollama_measure_pending: Apply first: the server is not running these settings yet.
admin.models.ollama_model_any: Any (loads what it is asked for)
admin.models.ollama_no_gpus: The cards are not known yet. Run ./home-stack ollama on the host once and they appear here.
admin.models.ollama_no_gpus_to_place: The cards are not known, so nothing was placed. Run ./home-stack ollama on the host once.
admin.models.ollama_removed: No longer on the list; the next Apply stops and removes: {units}.
admin.models.ollama_save_apply: Save and apply to the host
admin.models.ollama_save_help: Saving changes the list. The servers change when it is applied to the host, which restarts the ones that changed and unloads what they hold.
admin.models.ollama_saved: Saved. Apply it to the host to restart the servers that changed.
admin.models.ollama_setup_not_followed: Not moved with its setup, which now runs a model it cannot use: {roles}. Pick another setup for it below.
admin.models.ollama_tasks_help: The tasks set to "Local Ollama" in the roles above. Pick a setup for each; the benchmark's score for that kind of task is beside it.
admin.models.ollama_trigger_missing: This page cannot restart servers on the host yet. Run this once on the host (it asks for your password), and Apply appears here:
admin.models.ollama_trigger_stale: The host's helper is from an older version. Run this on the host again to update it:
admin.models.ollama_unpinned: Not pinned to a card: {ids}. Ollama then places models wherever there is room, and may split one across both cards.
admin.models.ollama_unplaced: Does not fit on any card: {ids}. Saved on the card with most room; lower a window or the slots, or remove a setup.
admin.models.ollama_unused: No role runs on it yet.
admin.models.ollama_vision_help: Ollama applies one parallel-slot count and one context length to every model it loads. A second server lets the vision model have a large window while the text roles keep several small fast slots. Leave empty and vision uses the main ollama.
admin.models.overrides: Set here, so it does not follow {parent}. Clear it to follow again.
admin.models.pi_probe_stale: the assistants still run {model}; deploy nanobot to test {configured}
admin.models.pi_probe_why: a short background task in pi: look something up and make a one-page PDF (takes up to three minutes)
admin.models.placement_elsewhere: Somewhere else entirely. This is the rescue, so it should not share a provider — or a machine — with the thing it rescues.
admin.models.placement_hosted: Hosted. This one reads or writes more than a model on your own hardware can hold, or somebody is watching a cursor while it thinks.
admin.models.placement_local: Local is the right answer here — nobody is waiting on it, the context stays small, and hardware you already own costs nothing per token.
admin.models.price_check_help: Prices move. The set this stack shipped with had one model at half what it costs now.
admin.models.reason.local: on your own hardware, nothing per token
admin.models.refresh_error: Could not refresh the prices ({detail}). The list below is the last one fetched.
admin.models.responses_refused: Not saved for {roles}: that service calls /v1/chat/completions, and OpenCode Zen serves this model on /v1/responses only.
admin.models.role_designer_why: A whole HTML page in one answer, print CSS and all (personas/designer.md).
admin.models.role_doctor_why: A profession, like Programmer and Teacher: health questions, read carefully and answered plainly. Its own model because each profession names one and uses it.
admin.models.role_documents_why: What Paperless's AI suggests a new document's title, tags, correspondent, type and date with. It reads the text Paperless got out of the scan, not the image, so any model that writes JSON will do -- and every page of every document goes through it, which is the strongest case in the house for a model that never leaves it. Left blank, Paperless's AI is off.
admin.models.role_events_measured: 2026-09-01: 519 chore turns and 112 location turns, average 25.8k tokens, largest 32,416, none above 60k.
admin.models.role_events_why: Chores coming due and people arriving home: the house asking Alfred to phrase something, rather than a person asking for anything. Nobody is waiting, and each one is a single short session -- so this is the household job that fits on your own hardware without a caveat.
admin.models.role_everyday_why: Ordinary chat. Somebody is waiting, and it runs more than anything except notification triage — so the input price, after caching, is most of the bill.
admin.models.role_fallback_why: The model every other hosted role swings onto when the one it asked for keeps answering with errors. It is not a cheaper tier or a second opinion -- it is the same job as Everyday Alfred, done on a bad day, so it needs to be able to do that job and it must not be a model already in use above. It may run on any provider -- and on a house with one provider it probably should run on another, because a fallback that shares a provider with every role goes down with it.
admin.models.role_legal_why: A profession: contracts and paperwork, where the whole document has to fit and the wording matters more than the speed.
admin.models.role_notifications_measured: 2026-09-02: the session now rotates every 40 turns and carries a digest forward, holding the prompt near 25k. Before that, 2026-08-17: 86k prompt tokens on average for a 21-token answer, because the session accumulates the whole day. Capping that history is worth ~10x any model swap.
admin.models.role_notifications_why: The highest-volume turn in the house by an order of magnitude and the smallest — two thirds answer SILENCE in eight tokens. Input price is the whole bill.
admin.models.role_powerful_why: When getting it right is worth more than getting it quickly: turns HomeCore marks as hard, and every turn inside a profession's chat that does not name a profession of its own. A wrong figure or a wrong command costs more than the extra seconds. Ordinary chat stays on the fast model. This is not background work -- see Sub-agents for that.
admin.models.role_programmer_why: Code review and diagnosis, over whole files (personas/programmer.md).
admin.models.role_subagent_powerful_why: The same work when it is complex or long-running -- research somebody asked for hours of, not a lookup. It gets the stronger model because nobody is waiting on a keystroke for it. Leave it empty to use the ordinary sub-agent model.
admin.models.role_subagent_why: What the assistant hands work to rather than doing it in the turn: a background task, a memory consolidation, the morning summary. Nobody is watching the seconds, but it makes a lot of calls, so the input price is most of what it costs.
admin.models.role_teacher_why: Guides, tests and mark schemes: long output, and a format to follow exactly (personas/teacher.md).
admin.models.role_titles_measured: 2026-09-10: ornith-1.5:9b, five real-shaped chats, median 0.29s, titles at least as good as qwen3.5:4b's at 0.20s — and no second model on the card.
admin.models.role_titles_why: A 3-to-6-word name for each conversation in the portal, asked for once per chat with a 24-token budget. Nobody waits for it and nothing depends on it, so the only thing that matters is that the model is already loaded: a separate one evicts something doing real work. Left blank, the portal uses the model the text roles keep resident. Thinking is switched off on the call, because a reasoning model spends the whole budget thinking and the chat never gets a name.
admin.models.role_vision_why: Camera frames and any photo somebody sends. Local by default, where the images never leave the house and cost nothing.
admin.models.roster_intro: Per million tokens. Anything on your own hardware costs nothing per token — it costs electricity.
admin.models.saved: Saved. The assistant picks it up on the next deploy.
admin.models.setup_in_use: {name}: not removed, a task still uses it -- pick another setup for it first.
admin.models.setup_unused: Not used by any task, so not running (≈ {gib} GiB when it is).
admin.models.setups_none: No model setups yet. Add one: a model, its window, cache and slots.
admin.models.show_all: Show all {n} models this role can run
admin.models.slot_image_high_why: Used when somebody asks for something to keep: a theme backdrop, a picture for a document. Slower and dearer per image, and worth it because the result is looked at.
admin.models.slot_image_normal_why: Everything else. Quick sketches, a thumbnail, an illustration in passing. This one runs far more often, so its price is the one that shows up on a bill.
admin.models.sources_intro: Each source is fetched separately and fails separately. Switching one off removes its models from the picker straight away.
admin.models.speech_intro: What the house listens and speaks with. Neither is a chat model: whisper's choice is a size, audio.cpp's is a package the service was deployed with. Both take effect on the next deploy of the service that reads them.
admin.models.speech_tts_help: Only a package audio.cpp was deployed with can be chosen; the voice inside it is picked on the Voice page.
admin.models.speech_tts_none: audio.cpp ships no TTS packages on this install — see the Voice page.
admin.models.speech_whisper_help: Smallest first. `small` is what a CPU-only compute host keeps up with; `large-v3-turbo` needs a GPU and hears far better. The weights are downloaded on first use.
admin.models.suggest_intro: The five cheapest that can do this job, priced against what this house measured the role spending in a month. Facts only — no catalogue publishes a quality score, so none is invented here.
admin.models.suggest_intro_assumed: The five cheapest that can do this job. Nothing has been recorded for this role yet, so the prices assume a million input tokens a month, none cached — a basis for comparing them, not a forecast. Facts only: no catalogue publishes a quality score, so none is invented here.
admin.models.suggests: What this page would put here
admin.models.tenants_help: These move with their own deploy: saving a change here asks for it at the top of the page. The bars above already count them on the card chosen.
admin.models.test_intro: Sends this role's model the kind of turn it actually serves — a hard count for harder turns, a triage it should answer with silence — and scores what comes back against checks that can be verified here. The rate is output tokens over the whole round trip, so it includes thinking the model does before answering; it is not a decode benchmark.
admin.models.test_no_model: No model is chosen for this role yet.
admin.models.test_unknown_role: That is not a role on this page.
admin.models.type_different: a different family from the rest
admin.models.why_this_group: Why these run where they do
admin.models.zero_cost_refused: Not saved for {roles}: a model that costs nothing is not for the assistant's unattended traffic.

admin.overview.hosts_intro: Where each part runs. They are all this machine unless you point one somewhere else.
admin.overview.settled: Everything is set up and deployed.
admin.overview.todo_intro: A few things still need you before the house is running.
admin.overview.todo_members: Nobody lives here yet. Add the first person to give them a login and their own assistant.

admin.overview.todo_pending: {n} service(s) changed here but not yet deployed: {names}

admin.plugins.add_help: A name on its own is looked for under the plugins directory; anything starting with / is taken as it is. It must hold a plugin.yml, and it must be outside this package — inside, a checkout would destroy it.
admin.plugins.deploy_admin: Added. It lives outside the plugins directory, so deploy the admin page once to let it read it.
admin.plugins.edit_help: The path on the machine that deploys. Correcting it here keeps the plugin where it sits in the list; nothing on disk is moved or deleted.
admin.plugins.err_already: That one is already on the list.
admin.plugins.err_no_deployer: The deployer could not be loaded, so this cannot be checked. Fix that first.
admin.plugins.err_vanished: That plugin is no longer in the list — it was removed while this page was open. Nothing was changed.
admin.plugins.heading: Plugins
admin.plugins.intro: A plugin is a directory outside this package with a plugin.yml in it. What it declares is built, deployed, checked and backed up exactly like anything that ships here — which is the difference between a plugin and a bookmark below.
admin.plugins.name: Plugin
admin.plugins.port_fixed: Fixed by the plugin — it writes this number itself, so changing it here would not reach the container.
admin.plugins.remove_confirm: Stop deploying {name}? The directory is left where it is.
admin.profile.actions_intro: Each of these acts on this person alone, and takes effect immediately — they are not saved with the settings above.
admin.profile.active_help: Switching someone off keeps the person, their id and everything they own; it drops their assistant instance. Removing is the destructive one.
admin.profile.birthdate_bad: That is not a date this page understands. Write it {format}.
admin.profile.birthdate_help: Written {format}. The assistant uses it to know how old somebody is and to say happy birthday.
admin.profile.hobbies_help: The assistant uses these to pick topics, gifts and examples that actually land.
admin.profile.hobbies_placeholder: one per line — football, K-pop, robotics…
admin.profile.intro: What the household's assistant should know about this person. Feeds their assistant's profile; the portal's family directory can hold the rest.
admin.profile.login_intro: The login for the household portal. Leave the password blank to keep the one they have.
admin.profile.login_none: This person has no way to sign in to the portal yet. Give them a login name and a password.
admin.profile.login_password_help: At least {n} characters. It is stored as a hash; nobody can read it back, including this page.
admin.profile.login_rename_warn: This login has conversations saved under it. Renaming carries them across, but anything else that recorded the old name — a scheduled job, an assistant session — keeps pointing at it.
admin.profile.notes_help: Anything the assistant should always or never do for this person.
admin.profile.notes_placeholder: e.g. is a child — keep language simple and age-appropriate
admin.profile.ntfy_partial: Saved, but the subscription did not reach: {where}. That phone keeps its old topics until this succeeds.
admin.profile.parents_help: A shared topic for the adults. Their phone subscribes to it alongside their own; the children's phones cannot read it.
admin.profile.programmer_help: Gives this person a coding agent with real file and git tools, in their own checkouts. Costs a container and a server process. Off, their Programmer stays on the assistant — the same profession, a different backend.
admin.profile.rel_conflict: {name}'s page says something different. From that side this should be {expected}.
admin.profile.relationships_help: What each other member is to this person, in the household's own words — “mother”, “younger brother”, “grandmother”. Every one of these has a twin on the other person's page.
admin.profile.remove_help: Their credentials go with them. Their id is never reissued, so nothing can inherit it — but their state stays on disk.
admin.profile.seed_note: This seeds the person's assistant on its first start. After that, what they teach the assistant in conversation wins — a deploy never overwrites it.
admin.profile.wa_linked: A phone is linked. Alfred can answer on WhatsApp.
admin.profile.wa_no_bridge: This member has WhatsApp switched on but no bridge is running yet. Deploy the assistants to create it.
admin.profile.wa_off: WhatsApp is off for this person, so they have no bridge and no pairing code. Tick “WhatsApp” in the settings above, save, then deploy the assistants — the code appears here once the bridge is running.
admin.profile.wa_qr_help: Have the phone ready: the code is replaced every few seconds and this keeps showing the current one. Scan it in WhatsApp → Settings → Linked devices → Link a device.
admin.profile.wa_qr_none: Waiting for the bridge to draw a code…
admin.profile.wa_restart_failed: The bridge refused the restart. Reload the page and try again.
admin.profile.wa_restart_help: Restarts the bridge so it draws a fresh code straight away, instead of waiting for the current one to expire.
admin.profile.wa_restarted: The bridge is restarting. Reload in a few seconds for a new code.
admin.profile.wa_unlink_confirm: Unlink this phone? Alfred stops answering on WhatsApp until a phone is scanned again.
admin.profile.wa_unlink_help: Throws away the linked-device credentials so another phone can be paired. Remove the entry from the phone's Linked devices list too, or it keeps a slot.
admin.profile.wa_unlinked: Unlinked ({count} file(s) removed). Scan a code to pair a phone again.
admin.profile.wa_unlinked_intro: No phone is linked yet, so Alfred cannot answer on WhatsApp. Scan the code below with the phone this member uses: WhatsApp → Settings → Linked devices → Link a device.
admin.profile.whatsapp_help: Gives this person's assistant a linked phone: their own bridge container, their own session, and the WhatsApp skill turned on for them. Somebody scans a QR code once. Off, they simply have no WhatsApp channel.
admin.secrets.heading: Credentials
admin.secrets.intro: Stored in secrets/smart-home-bot.env on this machine, never in version control. Values are write-only here: once set, this page shows only whether a key is present.
admin.secrets.members_intro: Created when a person is added and deleted when they are removed. The assistant secret is generated for you; the document-archive token comes from the button on the Household page.
admin.secrets.model_key_help: The one credential this stack cannot generate, and the only one that leaves your network.
admin.secrets.models_intro: One key per service you want to use. Nothing here is required together — pick per job on the Models page: the GPU in the cupboard for notifications, a flat plan for everyday chat, whatever is best at code for the programmer.
admin.secrets.models_note: OpenCode Zen is the one this stack recommends: billed per token, against the Zen endpoint and not the flat Go plan, whose traffic rules this stack's round-the-clock unattended load does not fit. An Ollama on your own hardware needs no key at all — set its address on the Site page.
admin.secrets.regenerate_warning: Regenerating a shared secret needs every service that uses it deployed again.
admin.services.heading: Included services
admin.services.house_only_help: Ticked, this service is not served from the cloud proxy at all — a request from outside gets a 404, not a login. Untick it only if you want it reachable from anywhere behind a password.
admin.services.intro: Turning a service off stops the deployer touching it and hides it from the portal. It does not remove anything already running — deploy again to apply.
admin.services.name: Service
admin.site.assistant_name_help: Used in its own prompts and on the pages that mention it. Applied on the next deploy. Folders and image names keep the old lowercase name, so nothing it has already saved for anybody moves.
admin.site.dns_intro: The names people type. Point them at this machine in your router or DNS. Nothing internal depends on them — the stack keeps working if they never resolve.
admin.site.dns_resolver_note: Copy the right-hand column into your DNS resolver — one A record per name. It is read from hosts: above, not a separate setting, so it follows a role when you move it.
admin.site.dns_service_off: {service} is not deployed, so nothing answers this name. The name is kept.
admin.site.domain_help: The DNS suffix your hosts answer to. No public domain is needed.
admin.site.heading: Site
admin.site.hosts_intro: Where each role runs. Everything on this PC by default (127.0.0.1); point a role at another address and only that role moves.
admin.site.name: House name
admin.site.name_help: Shown as the title on every screen.
admin.site.paths_absolute: A path has to be absolute — it is read on another machine, where this page's working directory means nothing.
admin.site.paths_intro: Absolute paths on the target machines, outside anything a deploy replaces. These are the trees to back up — see docs/backups.md.
admin.site.paths_machine_help: On one PC, «All machines» is the only entry there is. Pick a machine only when that one keeps things somewhere else — a second disk, a VPS with no /mnt.
admin.site.paths_role_help: Where {role} keeps things. Matching «All machines» exactly is how you put it back to sharing.
admin.site.timezone_help: Container clocks stay UTC; anything shown to a person is converted to this.
admin.site.voice_help: Piper is built into the voice gateway and is always there; audio.cpp needs its service switched on. "default" is the engine's own voice. Extra Piper voices are dropped into config/home-voice/voices as an .onnx and its .onnx.json, and appear here once they are. Saving does not change anything until home-voice is deployed — the page will offer.
admin.site.voice_intro: What Alfred speaks with on the voice panels and in announcements.
admin.status.behind_help: A file in the service's directory is newer than its container. Normal on a machine somebody is working on.
admin.status.idle_help: Switched on in the config with no containers running. Either it was never deployed, or it is meant to be off.
admin.status.lede: What is running, and what is running behind the configuration.
admin.status.pending_help: A setting was saved and nothing has deployed it. This is the one that needs you.
admin.status.stale_help: The image tag points somewhere else now, so this container is a build nobody replaced. Two units building the same tag do this.

admin.status.verdict_ok: All {n} services are up and current.
admin.status.verdict_pending: {n} service(s) have a saved change nothing has deployed:

admin.voice.backend_pending: Chosen: {chosen}. The container is still running {running} — deploy audio-cpp to change it. Measurements below are from whichever is actually running.

admin.voice.heading: Voice
admin.voice.heard_help: Words that survived a round trip through the house's whisper: the middle word of each sentence, then the first. A model can be fast and unintelligible.
admin.voice.intro: What Alfred sounds like, and the speech models on this machine. These are files here, not an account somewhere — the Models page is for the ones that think, this one is for the ones that talk and listen.
admin.voice.model_help: The file audio.cpp speaks from. The voice above is a style inside it — supertonic ships ten, M1–M5 and F1–F5, with M1 the default. Most other packages have one.
admin.voice.models_help: Ticking a package downloads it on the next deploy of audio-cpp. Removing deletes its files here and takes it off the list, so it does not come back.
admin.voice.models_intro: Everything audio.cpp can serve. Tick what it should offer — the caller names one per request, so several can be on at once. Untick to stop serving; remove to get the disk back.
admin.voice.preview_cold: {cold}s cold (loading the model, paid once after a restart)
admin.voice.preview_fell_back: That engine did not answer — you are hearing {engine}, which is what the house would fall back to.
admin.voice.preview_took: {synth}s to speak {audio}s of audio (×{rtf} real time — under 1 is faster than you listen)
admin.voice.pruned: {n} package(s) no longer served were deleted, freeing {mb} MB.
admin.voice.remove_confirm: Delete the files for {id}? It will also stop being served.
admin.voice.remove_last: {id} is the only one of its kind left. Removing it would leave the runtime unable to do that job at all — tick another first.
admin.voice.runtime_help: cuda builds a different, much larger image and needs the card ticked as well — measured here: 187 MB and 2.50 s a line on the CPU, 2.89 GB and 0.07 s on an RTX 3060, in 637 MiB of it. Piper stays underneath whatever you choose.
admin.voice.runtime_intro: Only used while the audio-cpp service is switched on, under Services.
